scenes.say: A driving model its README says an agent wrote, trained on labels no human drew. What does it see, and how does it pick a path?

scenes.headline: How eight cameras become one driving plan
scenes.sub: METEOR, a surround-camera network from TIER IV
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Aldous! Meteor is a driving network from Tier Four. Let's follow eight camera images to a planned path.

scenes.title: Two ways to drive
scenes.say: Chapter one. Two ways to drive.

left.title: Modular stack
left.say: The classic stack is a chain of modules. Each arrow is a message a human designed, and anything not in it is lost.

right.title: One network
right.say: Meteor is one network: cameras and speed in, a path out. But it keeps depth, boxes and lanes as outputs you can inspect.

steps.say: The video from the post. Eight cameras with predicted segmentation and boxes, and predicted depth for every view.
On the right, the bird's-eye map: road, lanes, other cars and the planned path. All from one forward pass.

scenes.title: Cameras into a grid
scenes.say: Chapter two. Cameras into a grid.

scenes.title: Depth decides which cells get a feature

legend: A flat grid around the car, one feature per cell
Plain projection paints the pixel along the whole ray
The depth head says where along the ray the surface is
The gate keeps the feature where depth agrees
A second camera agrees; cameras are averaged by weight
params.depthLabel: Depth probability per bin along the ray

steps.say: Lay a flat grid on the ground around the car. Meteor's is eight hundred by five hundred cells. Here, a toy.
steps.term: BEV: a bird's-eye grid around the car

steps.say: One pixel's ray crosses many cells, so plain projection smears a parked car down the road behind it.
So the network also predicts depth: for every pixel, a probability over sixty-four distance bins. Here it peaks at the car.
Each cell takes the feature weighted by that probability, plus a small floor. Only the car's cell keeps it.
A side camera agrees. The grid stores the weighted average across all eight cameras, with no learned weights in this step.

scenes.title: The gate, per camera and cell

parts.note: depth head's probability at the cell's range
parts.say: The weight is the probability that the surface lies at this cell's range.

parts.note: a floor, so no cell gets exactly zero

scenes.say: Every grid point sits at height zero. The lift assumes a flat world.

steps.say: The project's diagram: one shared ResNet backbone, feeding segmentation, detection and depth heads.
Depth and context meet in the lift.
Every bird's-eye task is a head on that grid, including the planner.

scenes.title: A small planner
scenes.sub: Three candidate paths and a rule-based checker

scenes.title: From the grid to a checked path

steps.say: Strided convolutions shrink the grid and average it to one vector. An MLP adds the car's speed.
Out come three candidate paths, six waypoints over three seconds, each with a confidence. A later attention pool adds a small correction.
steps.term: Waypoint: a target position at a future time

steps.say: Three paths, so a fork does not average into the median. The most confident one goes to a guardrail.
The guardrail checks it against the network's own boxes, forecasts, traffic light and lanes. A failure vetoes it and stops in lane.

scenes.label: of the released network's weights are the planner
scenes.note: 4,521,408 of 54,060,013; the ResNet trunk alone is 21.28M
scenes.say: Counting the released checkpoint, the planner is about eight percent of the weights. The rest exists to see.

scenes.title: Labels and agents
scenes.sub: Who drew the ground truth, and who wrote the code

scenes.title: The autolabel factory
scenes.say: Twelve heads need twelve kinds of ground truth. A pipeline makes it all from recorded drives.

items.say: The planner's target is where the car actually went next.
Lanes come from LiDAR points coloured by segmentation masks, accumulated over the whole drive.
A LiDAR box is kept only if a camera confirms it.
Bad weather is re-rendered from real scenes, labels intact. No human labels, but not self-supervised either.

steps.say: The factory's output for one scene, every label generated from the recording.

scenes.title: The bug an automated judge missed

steps.say: Per the README, Claude wrote the code and ran training in rounds, each judged automatically. For two months, a cache bug fed the planner zero history.
steps.term: Round: one day-long training run, one change

steps.say: With real history, trajectories got thirty-three to thirty-eight percent worse.

steps.note: 107 to 83 ms on the Orin with history baked out
steps.say: So the release is single-frame. The judge never checked that input was non-zero.

scenes.title: Does it hold up?
scenes.say: Chapter five. Does it hold up?

scenes.label: parameters in the released checkpoint; the launch post said 16 million
scenes.note: counted from the checkpoint's tensors, without running it
scenes.say: The post said sixteen million parameters. The released checkpoint has fifty-four million.

scenes.credit: AutoE2E, from Shinpei Kato's post on X

steps.say: Its comparison, Auto E to E, plans in green over the human's purple path. Both are scored open loop, over footage the plan never changes.

scenes.title: What stands between this and a car

items.say: Its closed-loop test chains plans over logged images that never react.
The deployed model sees one frame at a time.
It was trained on one sensor rig, mostly on Japanese roads.
And its model card says it must not control a vehicle on public roads.

scenes.text: A big open perception network, a small planner and a rule checker on top. FSD is a whole system.
scenes.say: Meteor is a strong open reference: big perception, a small planner, a rule checker. Open-source FSD it is not.

scenes.say: Depth decides where features land. The planner is small. And the labels come from machines, not people.
